props.title: The Kiss
props.initialSlug: Greta Garbo shines in scandalous love triangle

sections.content: The Kiss marks a pivotal moment in cinema history as one of the last great silent films before talkies took over. Greta Garbo's magnetic screen presence drives this sophisticated melodrama about a married woman caught between duty and passion. The film showcases MGM's peak silent-era production values and director Jacques Feyder's European sensibilities. It shares DNA with other late silent masterpieces like Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) and The Crowd (1928), where visual storytelling reached incredible heights just before synchronized sound changed everything.

sections.content: The film's sophisticated handling of adult themes pushed boundaries for 1929, dealing frankly with marriage, infidelity, and passion in ways that would soon be restricted by the Production Code. Garbo's performance as Irene Guarry showcases the height of silent film acting technique - conveying complex emotions through subtle expressions and gestures. This approach influenced later femme fatale performances in films like Double Indemnity (1944) and Sunset Boulevard (1950).

Director Jacques Feyder brought European artistic sensibilities to Hollywood, evident in the film's moody lighting and psychological complexity. The Kiss demonstrates the international cross-pollination happening in late 1920s cinema, similar to F.W. Murnau's work on Sunrise (1927) and Paul Leni's The Man Who Laughs (1928). These European directors helped elevate American filmmaking beyond simple entertainment. SUBHEAD: The Transition to Sound

sections.content: The Kiss represents the end of an era, released as Hollywood frantically converted to sound production. While other studios rushed out awkward part-talkie hybrids like The Jazz Singer (1927), MGM took a more measured approach, letting masters like Garbo and director Feyder create one last purely silent masterpiece. The film's commercial success proved audiences still appreciated silent artistry even as The Broadway Melody (1929) ushered in the musical era.
